newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Yachting: Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Yachting: Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.

text.p: By Peter Campbell*
CELEBRATING AUSTRALIA DAY AFLOAT

As they have been doing for more than 160 years, Australians will celebrate our national day afloat at Australia Day regattas on Sunday, January 26, particularly on Sydney Harbour and Geelong's Corio Bay.

These two vast waterways have been venues for Australia Day regattas -- or Anniversary Regattas as they were once called -- since the first public festivities were held to commemorate the arrival of the First Fleet.
These events included races between the few privately-owned yachts, working skiffs and rowing races between the tough watermen of Australia's then two largest ports.

Sydney's Australia Day Regatta on Sunday will mark 161 years of annual celebrations on the harbour -- a remarkable and unprecedented continuity for an organised sailing regatta. Geelong's regatta extends over three days, with the Australia Day Weekend on Corio claimed to be the largest annual regatta in the nation.
Some 1,500 yachts are expected to take part, with passage races from the Port Phillip Bay clubs always a feature.

Significantly, the 161st Australia Day Regatta has been expanded far beyond Sydney Harbour for 1997, with major regattas planned on Sunday for Pittwater and Botany Bay. Others will be held on the Parramatta River, the Lane Cove River at Hunters Hill, at Iron Cove, Rose Bay, Manly Cove, Port Hacking and to the north at Wangi on Lake Macquarie.
On a lake at Homebush, adjacent to the Olympic site, there will even be an Australia Day regatta for radio-controlled model yachts.

A large fleet of ocean racing yachts will sail with the Cruising Yacht Club in the ocean race from Sydney Harbour to Botany Bay and return for the prestigious City of Sydney Sesquicentenary Cup, starting off Clark Island at 11 a.m. and finishing in Farm Cove, just near the Opera House, in mid to late afternoon.

Olympic class yachts will be racing at several regattas, with Soling keelboats at Manly and the new Australian-designed skiff class, the 49er, sailing out of Rose Bay along with Lasers and 470-class dinghies. Rival 18-footer fleets will also be racing together for the Lord Mayor's Cup.

Adding to the significance of the 161st annual Australia Day Regatta and the celebration of Australia Day Afloat, regatta sponsors Philips Electronics will distribute an Australian Red Ensign -- the national maritime flag -- to each yacht or pleasure boat on the harbour on Sunday.
This has been done on JUSTUS VEENEKLASS, chairman and chief executive of Philips Australia, Dutch-born but a fiercely patriotic Australian.

Apart from the 161st Australia Day Regatta on Sunday, other major events on the Harbour will be include the Tall Ships Race, the Ferry Marathon and the Flags Afloat Parade from Rose Bay to Darling Harbour in early evening.
TERRA FIRMA MAKES UP FOR LOST RUDDER

The 1995 Telstra Sydney-to-Hobart race winner Terra Firma made up for losing its rudder in the recent bluewater classic by rewarding her owners, young Melbourne computer software company partners SCOTT CARLILE and DEAN WILSON, with a fine overall performance in the International Measurement System (IMS) racer division of last week's Port Phillip Regatta.

The nine-race series of bay races run by various clubs began life as the Petersville Regatta, then became the highly promoted Nissan Regatta, but this year the Victorian Yachting Council was unable to obtain a naming rights sponsor.
Support with trophies did, however, come from Hewlett Packard and, despite limited promotion, the regatta attracted a large, high-quality fleet.

These included the first, second and fourth-placed yachts overall in the Sydney-to-Hobart, GIORGIO GJERGJA'S Ausmaid from Melbourne and the Sydney yachts BZW Challenge, owned by RAY ROBERTS, and Atara (ROGER HICKMAN). Also in the fleet was the veteran maxi from Sydney, grazier TONY PAOLA'S beautiful Condor.

However, the locals proved too skillful on Port Phillip, with Terra Firma, scoring a comfortable overall win from JLW Chutzpah, skippered by Collins Street dentist BRUCE TAYLOR, and the little sloop Atria, skippered by its designer, ROBERT HICKS for owner GILBERT FORD, the Gold Coast-based heart surgeon.

Ausmaid had to be content with fourth overall, but the crew was happy enough to beat their arch-rivals aboard BZW Challenge. This came after the news that ROBERTS had lodged an appeal against the race jury's decision in the Sydney-to-Hobart in awarding his Corel-45 only 33 minutes instead of the sought-after two hours redress for time lost in searching an area where a flare had been sighted on the second night of the Hobart race.
If upheld and the full two hours is granted this could dramatically change the official IMS overall results of the Sydney-to-Hobart.

The other major winner of the Port Phillip Regatta was veteran Sandringham sailor and Melbourne businessman LOU ABRAHAMS with his Bashford/Howison-41 Seaview Challenge Again. ABRAHAMS, who had returned to Melbourne after this 34th Sydney-to-Hobart, sailed Challenge Again to six wins out of nine races in the IMS cruiser racer Division to score yet another overall success in this regatta, which he has not missed since its inception.
AMERICA'S CUP REGATTA IN AUCKLAND
America's Cup interest is warming up again New Zealand, with the announcement of the major sponsors for the defence of the Cup in 2000 and a mini-America's Cup regatta in Auckland in April this year.

New Zealand's two Black Magics -- NZL32 and NZL38 -- took to the water as Team New Zealand revealed the Family of Five sponsors who will provide much of the mainstream funding for New Zealand's defence. Lotto, Steinlager, Telecom New Zealand, Television New Zealand Toyoto New Zealand have all signed on, with all but Telecom New Zealand having been involved when the Kiwis won the cup back in May, 1995.

Meanwhile, four syndicates from the United States, Britain and France have confirmed that they will contest a Louis Vuitton Cup-style elimination series, with the winner challenging Team New Zealand in the final match.

The six-day regatta, from April 1-6, will be the feature event of a series of Road to America's Cup regattas which Team New Zealand is planning for every summer leading to its defence of the Cup in February and March 2000.

The syndicates to race in Auckland this April will be representing challenges from the New York Yacht Club and San Fransisco Yacht Club in the U.S., Britain's Royal Dorset Yacht Club and France's Societe Nautique Grau du Roise (Port Camargue).

The New York Yacht Club, the Challenger of Record for America's Cup 2000, will also race Team New Zealand in one-on-one tests in Wellington from March 5-9 and Auckland from March 25-29 in the other two events planned for 1997.
With the late entry deadline for America's Cup challenges set for May 14, there is still no sign of an Australian Challenge for 2000.

JOHN BERTRAND is out of contention, RAY ROBERTS has given no indication of his success in gaining sponsorship, and SYD FISCHER, as always, is tight-lipped about any plans he may have. His current yachting plans are directed towards the Admiral's Cup at Cowes, England, in July and August this year.
WHITBREAD STOPOVER CONFIRMED

As we reported last Friday, New South Wales premier BOB CARR officially announced that day that Sydney would be the second Australian stopover, following Fremantle, for the 1997-98 Whitbread Round-the-World Race.

This was something we had known for the past year or more, and the premier added little information other than saying how New South Wales had worked to upstage Victoria in getting Sydney as the stopover.
The same, he said, applied to Sydney being host for the World Youth Sailing Championships in January 2000.

In fact, the New South Wales government did little but procrastinate about giving some small support to an event that will bring millions to the state and city. The real work to gain the Whitbread Race came from Sydney yachtsmen IAN TRELEAVEN and PETER BUSH, along with yachting journalist ROB MUNDLE.

What will happen during the Whitbread stopover in Sydney will be establishment of a Whitbread Race village at the current site of the temporary casino at Daring Harbour to berth the yachts and provide a wide variety of information and entertainment.

The yachts, due in Sydney about December 22 this year, will finish the leg from Fremantle off the Sydney Opera House, with the race re-start by the fleet of 15-20 yachts happening off Lady Macquarie's Chair on January 4, when they head for Auckland.
*Peter Campbell is the editor of Offshore Yachting magazine.
